title: Electroplated copper-manganese alloy that grows its own barrier
idea: Combine TSV electroplating with barrier formation: plate Cu-0.5%Mn from a non-aqueous or ionic-liquid bath onto an electroless seed; a 350 C anneal drives Mn to the oxide liner forming a few-nm MnSiO3 barrier and leaves pure Cu, deleting the argon-sputtered Ta/TaN barrier.
why: TSV cost and HBM area tax: removes a rare-gas PVD tool and enables thinner, higher-aspect TSVs with smaller keep-out zones.

title: Second-life DRAM: retired server DIMMs reborn as CXL pools
idea: Eliminate new wafers for the capacity tier: strip DDR4/DDR5 chips from decommissioned servers, screen with burn-in and row-hammer tests, and mount them behind CXL Type-3 controllers that translate protocol and map out weak rows.
why: Huge volumes of DRAM are retired yearly; reusing it as a slower tier raises usable supply with zero fab capex and spares new DDR5/HBM for hot data, at ~5-10x lower cost/bit than today's 4x contract price.

title: Core-rope wired-sum: shared magnetic cores reduce partial sums in-package
idea: Like Apollo rope memory threading dozens of wires through one core, route the current-mode outputs of 8-16 processing-in-memory chiplets through shared thin-film magnetic cores on the substrate, so one secondary winding carries the analog sum and a single host ADC reads the reduced value.
why: Fact 5: in-package accumulate/all-reduce of partial dot products moves one value instead of N (8-16x less reduction traffic) with zero active circuitry; precision ~6-8 bits, limited by core linearity and drive matching.

title: Firefighter's bucket brigade: charge-domain CCD data bus on interposer
idea: A bucket brigade passes water hand to hand: move bits across the interposer as packets of charge clocked through CCD-like transfer gates, like a camera readout, instead of charging full wires to rail.
why: Charge transfer needs no full-wire CV2 swing: claimed 5-10x lower energy per bit for long memory buses where data-movement power is 20-25% of the accelerator's.

title: Taffy-pulled wire-in-glass preform sliced into through-glass-via wafers
idea: Stack copper-cored glass capillaries into a preform, draw it down 500x on a fiber tower, re-bundle and redraw (as multicore fiber is made), then slice the rod like salami into 100 um glass discs. Each disc holds millions of 2 um-pitch through-glass vias formed in one draw.
why: Laser drilling plus plating of glass vias is slow and costly; drawing yields interposer cores with ~10^7 vias/cm2 at fiber-tower throughput, for denser and cheaper memory interposers.

title: Parameter change: chilled DRAM zones cut refresh bandwidth theft
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter changes: give DRAM its own 10-20 C coolant loop on a cold plate separate from the 60 C compute loop, built from existing chiller hardware. Retention roughly doubles for every ~10 C drop, so the refresh interval can stretch 4-8x through standard temperature-controlled refresh modes. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Refresh (fact 3): bandwidth lost to refresh falls from 10-20% to ~2-4%, and refresh energy (16-33% of idle power) falls ~4x, giving more usable bandwidth from the same chips.

title: Bit-plane memory layout for progressive-precision fetch
idea: MINIFY bits moved by storing tensors bit-plane by bit-plane (all MSBs together, then the next plane, and so on), so an accelerator fetches only the top N planes that the current layer or token needs.
why: Data-movement energy and effective capacity: 2-4x fewer bits moved for inference, with precision chosen per access.

title: Coarse pitch with 224G SerDes on organic substrate
idea: MAGNIFY bump pitch back to ~150-400 um and MAGNIFY lane speed to 224 Gb/s PAM4, attaching commodity LPDDR/DDR chiplets to accelerators on plain organic substrate with no silicon interposer.
why: Capital intensity and CoWoS bottleneck: memory bandwidth from abundant substrate capacity; claims ~5x cheaper packaging per GB at ~3-5 pJ/bit.

title: Blow-away ESD shunts after bonding to strip I/O capacitance
idea: Ideal: die-to-die wires with zero parasitic load. Closest achievable: replace each inter-die pad's ESD diode stack (~0.2-0.5 pF) with one shared sacrificial shunt network that protects only during handling and bonding, then laser- or electrically fuse it open after the stack is sealed, leaving ~10 fF bond loads.
why: Facts 5 and 6: link energy scales with C, so removing ESD load cuts per-bit energy 5-10x on hybrid-bond and TSV lanes and shrinks pad area so more lanes fit per mm2.

title: Seeded procedural weights regenerated beside the multiply units
idea: A tensor's true storage cost is its Kolmogorov complexity, not its size. Train models whose matrices are W = PRNG(seed per block) times a few learned coefficients, and place LFSR/hash generators next to the MAC arrays to regenerate weights on the fly, so memory holds seeds and coefficients only.
why: 10-100x fewer stored and moved bytes, so cost per effective GB ~100x lower; trades training effort and some accuracy.

title: Bubble-memory rotating field shifts data through stacks without wires
idea: As bubble memory moved every bubble with one rotating in-plane field, wrap a two-phase package coil around a stack of dies carrying permalloy T-bar/chevron domain-propagation tracks, so one resonant global field shifts data from every tier toward a port die at once, crossing tiers by magnetostatic coupling through thin bond layers.
why: Facts 5/6: per-wire CV^2 switching is replaced by one shared field whose energy is recovered in a high-Q LC tank, and no TSVs are needed for bulk sequential transfer; claimed 3-5x lower movement energy if massive parallelism compensates for MHz-class shift rates.

title: Return addresses, not data: similarity search inside the stack
idea: Reverse the query direction: the host sends a query vector, a dot-product/top-k engine in the base die scans stored keys at internal bandwidth, and it returns only the k indices and scores; the host then fetches just those k values.
why: Long-context KV caches and vector databases (facts 5, 8): link traffic drops 10-100x because keys never leave the stack.

title: Fax-machine run-length coding compresses sparse traffic on memory bus
idea: Adapted from Group 3 fax Modified Huffman/RLE: a 180 nm codec on the memory buffer encodes zero runs and repeated values in activations, sparse weights and KV-cache before they cross the bus and land in DRAM.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and effective capacity: ReLU and sparse tensors are often 50-90% zeros, so 2-5x fewer bits are moved and stored.

title: 1980s DNQ-novolac i-line strategy for PFAS-free domestic interposers
idea: Standardize HBM interposers and RDL at >=1.5-2 um lines on non-chemically-amplified DNQ-novolac resist and i-line steppers, 1980s tooling that is cheap, available used and buildable in the U.S., and design memory interfaces wide and slow enough to fit those rules.
why: Constraint and US manufacturability: DNQ resists contain no PFAS PAGs; i-line steppers cost ~$3-5M versus $20M+ for ArF, enabling domestic interposer capacity under a shared open standard.

title: Terahertz in-package broadcast: one transmission feeds every chiplet
idea: A wire costs energy per destination; a radiated wave costs once for N receivers. Put 300 GHz on-chip antennas on the HBM base die and every compute chiplet inside a metal-lidded package cavity acting as a waveguide, broadcasting weights or shared activations to all chiplets simultaneously.
why: For multi-chiplet weight broadcast, energy per delivered bit falls ~N (4-16x) versus point-to-point copies (fact 5).

title: Coaxial TSV whose liner doubles as on-die decoupling capacitor
idea: Combine the HBM power TSV with a deep-trench MIM capacitor: build each power via as a coaxial stack (Cu core / ZrO2-Al2O3 high-k liner / doped-Si or TiN outer shell) so the ~50 um via sidewall supplies roughly 5-10 pF of decap. Thousands of power TSVs then become the stack's decoupling bank and the periphery's planar MOS decap arrays are deleted.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) and HBM TSV keep-out tax: reclaims ~3-6% die area and lowers PDN noise so VDDQ margin and I/O energy drop ~5-10%; keep-out zones do double duty.

title: Echo: DRAM die backscatters host carrier, never drives line
idea: Forced 'echo': the host sends a continuous carrier, and the DRAM die only switches its termination impedance to reflect a modulated echo (RFID-style backscatter). The slow-transistor DRAM process never has to build high-speed drivers.
why: DRAM-side I/O energy and periphery area; transmit power moves to the logic node, which does it 5-10x more efficiently.

title: Pneumatic tube: coolant microchannels double as sub-THz waveguides
idea: Mail tubes carry capsules, so the interposer's dielectric-coolant microchannels are shaped as rectangular waveguides and carry 200-300 GHz modulated carriers between chiplets while also cooling the HBM stack. A single channel provides both heat removal and a multi-10 Gb/s data path.
why: Long-reach (2-5 cm) chiplet links at <1 pJ/bit without extra routing layers; lets memory sit farther from hot compute and still be cooled.

title: MEMS relay computers died of contact wear; relays pool memory instead
idea: Berkeley-style MEMS relay logic failed because contacts wore out within ~1e9 cycles and switched too slowly for logic. Memory pooling switches only when allocations change (minutes), so build an in-package crossbar of electrostatic poly-Si relays with TiN/carbon contacts (no Ru, Pt or W) that physically re-wires memory chiplets between compute dies, with zero standby power and no SerDes.
why: Stranded memory: package- or board-level DRAM follows whichever die needs it, reclaiming 15-30% stranded capacity with no added latency once connected; Si, Ti, N and C only.

title: Seed-regenerated weights: memory interface synthesizes matrices from tiny seeds
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Store each weight block as a PRNG seed plus a few combination coefficients; an LFSR basis generator in the memory base die regenerates the block on the fly at read time, trading cheap logic gates for stored bits.
why: Capacity and data movement: ~8-12x fewer stored bits for weights, so ~10x model per GB of DRAM; logic gates cost far less than DRAM bits.

title: KryoTech fixed: hermetic Peltier-cooled DRAM tile trades refresh for density
idea: KryoTech's sub-ambient PC cooling (1990s) died on condensation and compressor cost. Cool only the low-power DRAM stack (a few W) to ~20 C with a thin-film thermoelectric inside a hermetically sealed dry-nitrogen package cavity while the logic stays at 85-100 C. Retention roughly doubles every ~10 C, so the tens-of-times longer retention can be spent on less refresh or a 30-40% smaller storage capacitor.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and the capacitor wall (fact 1): refresh energy and bandwidth loss largely eliminated, or Cs relaxed for lower-aspect-ratio, cheaper etch, at ~1-3 W of Peltier power per stack.

title: Push-streaming DRAM: memory runs the schedule, host stops asking
idea: Invert 'memory is a passive slave waiting for commands': the compiler uploads a static access program (tensor walk, bank interleave, refresh slots) into a tiny sequencer on the HBM base die, which activates banks and pushes data down a unidirectional link in fixed slots; the host keeps only a credit/abort lane, no command/address bus.
why: Removes CA pins and host scheduling logic (~15-25% of PHY pins/power), kills turnaround bubbles and lets the base die slot refresh and row-hammer mitigation into idle windows; ~1.3x effective bandwidth for static AI graphs.

title: Uploaded access programs delete the DRAM command bus
idea: Ideal: no requests at all, data simply arrives on time. Closest achievable: compilers for static AI graphs emit a timed access program (tile addresses, strides, bank schedule) once per layer, and a tiny sequencer in the base die replays it so the per-access command/address bus and controller queues vanish.
why: Facts 5 and 7: command/address bumps (~20% of HBM signal bumps) become data bumps, GPU controller area and energy shrink, and conflict-free schedules push bandwidth utilization toward 95%.

title: Resonant charge-recovery drivers that recycle bus wire energy
idea: Po: wires give their energy back. Drive memory data lines through small on-die inductors so each line resonates; line capacitance swings adiabatically and most of the CV2 charge returns to the tank instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Breaks the CV2 voltage floor on interface wires; 2-4x lower link energy per bit at the same swing.

title: Roll memory like a film capacitor with sprayed end contacts
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Transfer DRAM device films onto a 10 um polyimide ribbon whose bus lines all exit at the two ribbon edges, wind it into a tight cylinder like a metallized-film capacitor, and arc-spray (Schoop) metal end caps that tie every turn's edge lines to power and a radial data comb.
why: Volumetric density with capacitor-industry roll-to-roll and winding tools that cost pennies per part; a 10 mm cylinder holds ~100x the silicon area of its footprint.

title: Pockels effect: thin-film lithium niobate modulators bonded on HBM base die
idea: Heterogeneously bond thin-film LiNbO3 microring modulators onto the HBM base die so the stack speaks optics directly at ~0.5-1 V drive and ~50 fJ/bit modulator energy; memory sits meters from the GPU over fiber with no electrical SerDes.
why: Frees memory from GPU beachfront and interposer area; ~1 pJ/bit end-to-end vs 3-4 pJ/bit electrical HBM at 10x+ the reach; enables pooled HBM.

title: Fraud-graph pointer chasing executed inside the memory stack
idea: Fraud-detection and social graphs are extreme pointer chasers with one useful word per hop. Put a tiny walker engine in the base die that follows pointer chains and returns only the final result, keeping every intermediate hop inside the stack.
why: Each hop otherwise crosses the PHY twice with a full burst; internal hops cost far less, ~10x lower energy per logical graph access and lower latency.

title: Goto parametron revival: phase-encoded links pumped by shared resonant clock
idea: Each link endpoint is a varactor parametric oscillator pumped at 2f by a package-wide resonant LC clock grid; a bit is the 0 or pi phase of the subharmonic oscillation, seeded by a tiny injection and amplified by pump energy, so there is no rail-to-rail driver.
why: Facts 5/10: sidesteps the CV^2 voltage floor because signal energy circulates in high-Q resonators and is mostly recovered; target <0.1 pJ/bit for die-to-die links versus ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit for today's parallel D2D PHYs.

title: Logic-die wordline segment drivers kill 128x page overfetch
idea: Overfetch exists because global wordlines are long and drivers are costly in DRAM process. Hybrid-bond a logic die whose fine-pitch bonds drive each 512-cell local wordline segment directly, so a 64 B read activates 64 B of cells instead of an 8 KB row.
why: Cuts random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward ~0.2 pJ (fact 8) and shrinks row-hammer aggressor exposure (fact 9).

title: Newspaper-press roll-to-roll interposer ribbons for memory rings
idea: Like a rotary newspaper press, make polyimide ribbons with 2-5 um semi-additive Cu lines roll-to-roll at ≤250 C. Use them to connect HBM-class stacks placed in a ring 2-5 cm around the compute die.
why: Ribbon cost per mm² is ~10x below silicon interposers, and the ring lifts the shoreline limit. That allows ~2x more stacks per accelerator at a modest pJ/bit penalty.

title: Stretchable-electronics liquid-metal bumps for warpage-free giant panels
idea: Stretchable wearables connect rigid chips with gallium alloy that never fatigues. Attach memory dies to large glass or organic panels with encapsulated eutectic gallium-indium microbump wells (30-50 um pitch) at room temperature, absorbing CTE mismatch and allowing rework by warming.
why: Warpage and reflow mismatch cap interposer and package size; room-temperature compliant joints allow 100-stack panels and rework, raising assembly yield.

title: Hermit-crab reuse: re-home DRAM from retired modules into CXL expanders
idea: Hermit crabs move into shells others have left. A U.S. reverse-logistics business does the same for retired server DIMMs and boards: robots desolder the DRAM packages, which are retested, speed-binned and graded for warranty, then re-mounted in high-capacity CXL memory expanders that hide their slower speed behind tiering.
why: Usable supply and U.S. manufacturability: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4/DDR5 modules a year; re-homing even 10% of that adds several % effective supply with near-zero wafer capital.

title: DNA-hybridization fluidic self-assembly of memory chiplets
idea: Chiplet bond pads and interposer landing sites carry different complementary DNA strands, so chiplets tumbled in a fluid bath bind only to their matching sites; a reflow then melts the solder and burns off the DNA. Thousands of known-good dies assemble in parallel instead of by serial pick-and-place.
why: Capital intensity and HBM yield (fact 6): makes many small, high-yield memory chiplets per package practical, cutting placement tool cost and time by roughly an order of magnitude.

title: In-package mm-wave radio bus replacing interposer wires
idea: Invert 'chiplets must be wired together': each memory and compute chiplet has 200-300 GHz on-chip antennas, the metal lid forms a closed cavity, and links share the medium by frequency division so any memory reaches any compute die without routing.
why: Eliminates interposer routing congestion and enables broadcast; targets ~1-2 pJ/bit at tens of Gb/s per channel without an interposer.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops keyed chiplets into substrate wells
idea: Invert 'chiplets must be placed by precision bonders': give memory and logic chiplets unique keyed shapes that settle into matching wells of a glass carrier in a liquid bath, with surface tension giving final alignment before batch bonding.
why: Removes dependence on imported high-precision bonders, assembling thousands of chiplets per minute on a low-capital U.S. line.

title: Noise-trained models let inference memory strip all ECC
idea: Shift the error budget from access time (ns) to training time (hours): models are trained with injected 1% bit flips on stored weights and KV entries, with exponent clamping, so inference memory runs with zero parity, zero decode latency and unprotected cheap cells.
why: Recovers the ~12.5% capacity and bandwidth spent on ECC bits and lets inference memory use 1%-BER cells with relaxed refresh (fact 3).

title: Electroluminescence: printed perovskite LED arrays drive thousands of slow parallel lanes
idea: Print perovskite micro-LED and photodiode arrays with ~10 um pixels on interposer film and image one onto the other through a fiber bundle; 10,000 lanes at 200 Mb/s give 2 Tb/s with plain NRZ and no SerDes.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): wide-and-slow optical lanes avoid SerDes power (sub-pJ/bit); perovskite stability at 80 C and speed are the risks.

title: Optical broadcast of one weight copy to 64 accelerators
idea: Invert 'each accelerator owns a private copy of the model': one memory pool streams weights once into a passive optical star coupler that splits the same light to 64 GPUs in lockstep; each GPU consumes the broadcast layer by layer and keeps only activations and KV in local HBM.
why: Weight replication is a large share of fleet HBM; broadcasting one copy cuts per-GPU weight capacity need by up to ~64x in data-parallel inference, freeing bits rather than making new ones.

title: Core-memory technician's threaded coil column broadcast bus
idea: Like wires threaded through a stack of ferrite cores: a single vertical column of aligned on-die spiral coils runs through all 16 dies of a stack, so the base die broadcasts commands and addresses to every die at once inductively, with no command TSVs.
why: Removes command/address TSVs and their keep-out area, so the per-die TSV tax drops and stacks with mismatched dies can be mixed; ~0.1 pJ/bit for broadcast.

title: Printed staircase sidewalls replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Invert 'vertical interconnect must be drilled through the die': stack DRAM dies offset like stairs and print fine conductive lines down the exposed steps with U.S.-made aerosol-jet printers (New Mexico), linking each die's edge pads to the base.
why: No TSV etch, fill or keep-out zones and no 30 um thinning; removes much of HBM's ~3x area-per-bit tax using domestic tools.

title: Single LED-cured nanoimprint defines via and trench for interposers
idea: Combine nanoimprint lithography with dual damascene: a two-tier stamp imprints via and trench together into a UV-curable dielectric cured by 365 nm LED arrays, followed by electroless seed and Cu plating. No scanner, no excimer laser, no argon PVD.
why: Interposer capital and neon exposure: 0.5-1 um L/S interconnect without DUV, halving lithography steps per metal level.

title: Mott transition: printed VO2 off-die ESD clamps strip I/O pad capacitance
idea: Print VO2 nanoparticle-ink clamps on the package substrate at each memory I/O; an ESD surge drives them metallic so they shunt the current, letting on-die ESD diodes (100-300 fF per pad) shrink to minimum size.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): pad capacitance dominates short-reach I/O CV^2, so ~50% less pad C cuts I/O energy in proportion; also frees periphery area (fact 7).

title: Homogeneity: maskless direct-write silicon interposers in 200 mm fabs
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: make interposers from silicon, which matches the dies' CTE, in idle 200 mm fabs, and pattern 2 um Cu RDL with maskless laser direct-imaging tools borrowed from the PCB industry. Interposers can then exceed the reticle limit without stitching and need no masks. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital, masks and the CoWoS chokepoint (fact 4): zero mask cost, and larger-than-reticle interposers fit more memory stacks, using depreciated 200 mm capacity.

title: Map-tile mipmapped KV cache: zoom only where needed
idea: Map apps load coarse tiles, then zoom in. Keep pooled summary keys for each 64-token block in HBM and score those blocks first. Full-resolution KV blocks come from CXL or flash only for the highest-scoring tiles.
why: Long-context KV caches fill most of HBM. Tile-based fetch could shrink the HBM KV footprint 4-8x with little accuracy loss.

title: Shingled staircase HBM wired by printed edge traces
idea: Po: holes in silicon are forbidden. Offset each DRAM die ~200 um like a NAND staircase and connect the exposed edge pads with aerosol-jet-printed copper traces running down the steps to the base die, giving a TSV-free stack with a few thousand edge links.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss), letting core dies cost like DDR5 dies while keeping a wide stacked interface.

title: Packaging inside the DRAM fab: wafers never leave the building
idea: Invert 'packaging is a separate offshore back end': run wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding of DRAM array wafers to base-logic wafers inside the U.S. DRAM fab (Idaho/New York) using its cleanroom, metrology and yield data.
why: Removes Asia OSAT round trips, cuts weeks of cycle time and unifies front/back-end yield learning; U.S. HBM-class memory becomes a single-site product.

title: Interposer made of DRAM: memory inside the substrate
idea: Box: planar 1T1C at relaxed F~25 nm x planar access x local SA x face-to-face hybrid bond x the interposer itself x DUV-only fab. The 2.5D interposer, today dead silicon, is fabricated as a reticle-stitched DRAM array with routing channels, and GPU/CPU chiplets hybrid-bond on top so each chiplet reads the gigabytes directly beneath it.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4) and data movement (fact 5): DUV-only node with zero EUV layers, reuses area already paid for, ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical access, ~10-20 GB per 2,500 mm2 interposer.

title: Memory scroll: dielets on flex coiled around the processor
idea: Box: DRAM dielets x standard x standard x fine-line polyimide ribbon x flexible substrate x roll-to-roll assembly. Dielets are bonded along a 2 m flex ribbon that coils around the processor package like a scroll, so attachable memory grows with the number of turns instead of the die's shoreline.
why: HBM shoreline limit: 3-5x more attachable capacity per package at DDR-like cost per bit.

title: Bit-plane-major tensor layout with on-demand mantissa streaming
idea: Po: throw data away before it moves. Store tensors bit-plane-major so the interface ships sign, exponent and top mantissa planes first; the accelerator requests lower planes only for tiles whose running error estimate exceeds a threshold, so most low bits never leave the DRAM.
why: 2-3x effective bandwidth and interface energy for inference, and less row overfetch per useful bit.

title: Origami accordion fold: one thinned DRAM strip folded into a stack
idea: Leave 8-16 DRAM dies joined in a strip on the thinned wafer, bridged by polyimide hinge RDL across the saw street. Fold the strip like an accordion into a stack, so the hinges carry the shared bus around the edges and no TSVs or microbumps are needed.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area/bit) and the 20-30% stacking yield loss from bump joins; claims ~2x usable bits per HBM wafer.

title: Ant-bridge glass chiplets: embedded glass bridges link memory and GPU
idea: Army ants build bridges only where the column must cross a gap. Likewise small glass bridge chiplets with 1-2 um lines are embedded in an organic substrate only under the GPU-to-memory edges, replacing both full silicon interposers and silicon EMIB-style bridges; the bridges are cut from large panels patterned with display-class lithography.
why: Cost and capital: bridge area is ~5-10% of an interposer and made on panels, so high-bandwidth memory packaging cost could fall ~40-60%.

title: Nokia-era embedded-die circuit boards hide DRAM inside processor substrate
idea: Adapted from 1990s HDI cellphone boards with laser microvias and embedded components: thinned DRAM dies are laminated inside the processor's organic substrate directly under the SoC and connected by stacked laser microvias.
why: Memory wires shrink to ~1 mm with no silicon interposer or TSVs; ~3-5x lower pJ/bit than DDR using PCB-class tools found in U.S. shops.

title: Co: CoFeB spin-torque nano-oscillators as in-package memory radios
idea: Use CoFeB/MgO magnetic-tunnel-junction spin-torque nano-oscillators (~100 nm, 5-40 GHz, tuned by bias current) as frequency-agile transmitters and detectors, giving each DRAM die its own wireless channel inside a shielded package so dies can sit without TSVs or bumps.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and packaging capital: each oscillator uses <1 um2 vs ~100 um2 for a TSV plus keep-out; speculative 1-2 pJ/bit.

title: Learned activation codecs inside the memory interface die
idea: Activations lie on low-dimensional manifolds, carrying far less information than 16 bits x width. Put a per-layer trained transform plus vector quantizer and entropy coder in the HBM/CXL base die so tensors are stored as 8-16x smaller codes and expanded on read, with error budgets set by training loss.
why: 10-30x effective capacity alone and ~100x when codes live on a NAND tier; trades accuracy and codec latency.

title: Penguin-huddle rotation: migrate hot data so no stack overheats
idea: Emperor penguins take turns between the cold edge and the warm centre of the huddle. Likewise the memory controller tracks per-stack temperature and periodically moves the hottest pages from stacks next to the GPU hotspot to cooler edge stacks, keeping every stack below the 85 C point where refresh doubles.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): avoids 2x refresh on hot stacks, recovering ~5-15% bandwidth and idle power for under 1% migration traffic.

title: Chip-first printed fan-out: interconnect printed directly onto placed dies
idea: Combine pick-and-place die embedding with aerosol-jet printing: DRAM and controller dies sit face-up in a molded panel and Ag/Cu nanoparticle inks plus polyimide dielectric are printed across die edges at 10-20 um lines, then sintered with near-IR diode lasers instead of xenon flash lamps.
why: Packaging capex and rare-gas exposure: zero masks, vacuum or rare gas; 3-5x lower capex for LPDDR/CXL memory modules on U.S. soil.

title: TTL-tagged writes: rows holding short-lived data skip refresh
idea: Match data lifetime to retention time: every write over the interface carries a time-to-live hint (activations microseconds, KV cache seconds), and rows whose data dies before 1% of cells decay are never refreshed. At 1% tolerance that unrefreshed window stretches from 64 ms to roughly 1 s.
why: Cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) ~70-90% for AI working sets.

title: DRAM in the socket cavity on the CPU package underside
idea: Use the package's other face: LPDDR packages mount on the land side of the CPU substrate inside a cavity in the socket and motherboard, putting memory ~2 mm under the die instead of 5 cm away on DIMMs. The top side stays free for cooling.
why: The short channel runs unterminated at ~1-2 pJ/bit vs 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5 (fact 5) while keeping DRAM out of the logic die's heat path.

title: Al: wire-bonded stacks behind DDR5 buffers free TSV capacity
idea: Build 128-256 GB RDIMMs/MRDIMMs from 4-8-die staggered stacks connected with Al/Cu wire bonds (NAND-style) behind the module's data buffers instead of TSV-based 3DS; the buffers hide the stub loads so the host still sees a standard DDR5 module.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV and stacking capacity is the HBM chokepoint; moving high-capacity server DIMMs off TSVs frees it for HBM at near-zero new capex.

title: Flash-on-logic hybrid bonding reads 100,000 planes in parallel
idea: NAND bandwidth is limited by narrow package pins, not the array: each plane senses 16 KB per ~20 us. Hybrid-bond a 3D NAND array wafer face-to-face with a compute wafer so 10^5 planes each get their own bonded bus, giving ~80 TB/s from a medium priced like flash.
why: HBM-class bandwidth at ~100x lower cost per GB for read-mostly weights; trades write endurance and 20 us latency.

title: Inline compute in CXL switches streams flash data, never landing
idea: Worsen: copy every dataset from SSD into DRAM, then to the GPU, then back. Flip: put streaming engines (decompress, filter, tokenize, embedding lookup) inside the PCIe/CXL switch so data flows flash to switch to accelerator SRAM at line rate and never lands in DRAM bounce buffers.
why: Data movement and DRAM demand: removes bounce buffers (tens of GB per server) and 2-3 copies per byte.

title: Laptop heat pipes etched into silicon spacers cool tall stacks
idea: Adapted from laptop heat pipes: the 1994 Bosch DRIE process etches sealed micro heat-pipe channels with wicking grooves into silicon spacer dies inserted in the memory stack. Filled with water or methanol, they carry heat sideways to the lid passively.
why: Thermal limits on stack height and hot refresh (fact 3): ~2-5x lower stack thermal resistance, allowing taller stacks and halving high-temperature refresh.

title: Hearing-aid LC resonant bus recycles line charge
idea: Hearing aids live on a 1-2 mW zinc-air budget. Pair each memory data line with an integrated on-package inductor so line plus inductor form a resonant tank; bits are sent as half-cycles of resonance, so the line's charge sloshes back instead of being dumped to ground each transition.
why: Recovering 80-90% of line CV2 cuts I/O energy ~5-10x; on short HBM-class wires this reaches ~10x lower interface energy per access (fact 5).

title: Descriptor-driven HBM: send access programs, not addresses
idea: Po: the processor never names an address. The GPU sends compact tensor access descriptors (base, strides, tile shape) to an address generator on the HBM base die, which walks rows in bank-friendly order and streams data back without per-line commands.
why: Frees command/address pins and link energy, and lets the stack fetch full rows usefully, cutting overfetch energy per useful bit.

title: Swiss-roll self-rolling capacitors enabling low-swing memory I/O
idea: Strained nanomembranes roll themselves into Swiss-roll capacitors embedded in the interposer, giving ~10x decoupling density. The quieter power delivery lets memory I/O drop to ~0.2 V swing.
why: I/O energy scales with V^2, so the claimed cut in link pJ/bit is ~3-5x.

title: Merging: content-addressed CXL appliance deduplicates shared KV prefixes
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging identical objects: a 28 nm CXL memory appliance hashes every 4 KB page written by many inference sessions (shared system prompts, common prefixes, replicated weights). It stores each distinct page once in commodity DDR4 and uses copy-on-write when a page diverges. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less: 2-5x effective capacity for multi-tenant LLM serving with shared prompts, built entirely from trailing-node logic and legacy DRAM.

title: Bedouin water reuse: resonant LC charge recovery on memory buses
idea: A desert nomad never pours water away: place spiral inductors on the interposer that resonate with each memory bus's capacitance, so energy sloshes back and forth between bit transitions instead of being dumped to ground at every edge.
why: Recovers ~60-70% of CV2 bus energy on HBM/DDR links (3-20 pJ/bit today); this is the voltage-floor problem solved in the interface instead of the cell.

title: Infrared light through silicon replaces vertical TSV signal lanes
idea: Substitute signal TSVs with bonded 1310 nm micro-LED / Ge photodiode pairs: silicon is transparent above 1.1 um, so each die shines data straight up through thinned neighbours, with Fresnel zone lenses etched in backside oxide to focus; only a few fat TSVs remain for power.
why: Fact 6: ~90% fewer signal TSVs and their keep-out area; contactless vertical signalling decouples bond yield from data integrity; ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit.

title: H: high-pressure deuterium anneal of finished stacks tightens retention
idea: Anneal completed HBM/3DS stacks in ~20 atm D2 at 250-300 C (within microbump limits) so deuterium diffuses to passivate Si/SiO2 interface traps in access transistors that drive trap-assisted leakage; the heavier isotope resists later hot-carrier depassivation.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): fewer weak cells means more stacks pass 32/64 ms retention at 85-95 C and fewer repair elements consumed, ~3-5% yield gain with interface unchanged.

title: Infrared light shines straight through silicon to wire 100 tiers
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so a vertical beam from a VCSEL array under the stack passes through every thinned tier; each tier reads with a thin Ge photodiode and writes with a free-carrier-absorption modulator on the same spot, making optical vias with no drilling.
why: Deletes TSV process cost (fact 6) so tier count is limited only by thinning: 100 tiers of 10 um in 1 mm targets 10x bits per footprint at HBM-like package cost.

title: Air-bridged interposer wires: vacuum dielectric cuts wire capacitance
idea: Wire capacitance per mm scales with permittivity, so oxide or polyimide (k 3-4) costs 3-4x the energy of vacuum. Build RDL lines over a sacrificial polymer and release it, leaving lines suspended on periodic posts in a sealed cavity like MEMS air bridges.
why: ~3x lower CV^2 for every interposer and chiplet bit, and faster lines allow lower swing (fact 5).

title: Publish-subscribe row broadcast turns overfetch into delivered prefetch
idea: Scarcity: no fetched bit may be wasted. When a row opens, the base die multicasts the row's other lines on a low-priority channel to every last-level-cache slice that registered interest in that address region (a subscription table in the base die) instead of discarding them at precharge.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): converting even 10-20% of overfetched lines into hits cuts energy per useful bit ~2x on irregular workloads.

title: Postal sorting office in the HBM base die
idea: A postal worker sorts mail by street before delivery: a 2k-entry CAM in the HBM base die holds incoming random 64 B requests for a few hundred ns, sorts them by bank/row and issues one activation per row batch, then scatters the replies back.
why: Attacks destructive read and 128x page overfetch (5.9 pJ per useful bit): claimed 3-6x fewer activations on graph and KV-cache traffic and ~40% lower energy per useful bit.

title: Open UCIe memory-chiplet standard to admit second-source DRAM makers
idea: Ideal: any memory die works with any processor. Closest achievable: define an open die-to-die DRAM chiplet interface (UCIe-based, with a standard base-die command set, thermal limits and test protocol) so new or smaller U.S. memory fabs can sell bare array chiplets into anyone's package without building their own base die or PHY.
why: Supply concentration and U.S. manufacturability: lowers the entry ticket from full HBM stacks to bare arrays and widens the supplier base beyond three companies.

title: Diatom biosilica: room-temperature porous low-k dielectric for panel RDL
idea: Diatoms grow hierarchically porous silica from silicic acid at room temperature using polyamines and silaffin-like peptides. The same chemistry deposits porous silica (k ~2.0-2.3) on organic or glass panels as the RDL dielectric, with no CVD tools and no high-temperature cure.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~30-40% lower wire capacitance than polyimide (k ~3.2) cuts interposer pJ/bit; it is a wet-bench process with no silicon wafer.

title: Genomics-grade sub-row activation with host column masks
idea: Genome aligners hammer memory with random 8-32-byte k-mer lookups. Add a column-mask field to ACT so segmented local wordline drivers fire only one 512 B segment of a row, and route only those bits to the I/O.
why: Attacks the 128x page overfetch (5.9 pJ per useful random bit): activating 1/16 of a row cuts random-access energy ~8-12x with a small periphery change.

title: Lego-stud reworkable press-fit sockets for HBM stacks
idea: Like Lego studs, electroplated Cu micro-pillars (~40 um pitch) on the interposer cold-press into compliant plated cups on the stack. A clamp frame holds them instead of solder, so stacks can be swapped, upgraded or harvested at room temperature.
why: One bad stack no longer scraps a $20k+ package, and memory can be reused across generations. Package yield and effective memory supply rise 10-20%.

title: Socketed HBM stacks on lithographic microspring arrays
idea: Invert 'memory is soldered permanently next to the GPU': HBM stacks press onto lithographic microspring contact arrays (~40 um pitch) on the interposer under a lid clamp, so stacks are tested in place, swapped on failure and reused in the next accelerator generation.
why: Turns HBM from a consumable bound to one GPU into a reusable asset; avoids scrapping a whole module when one stack fails and adds 1-2 extra service lives to each stack.

title: Phone vapor-chamber layers laminated between HBM dies
idea: Borrow the smartphone vapor chamber. Thin, sealed two-phase micro-chambers (wicked Cu mesh, water) sit between groups of core dies, with TSV bundles passing through sealed pillars. They spread heat sideways to a cold plate at the stack edge.
why: Heat limits HBM height and drives up refresh, because hot cells leak faster. Lateral spreading 3-5x better allows taller stacks and halves extra high-temperature refresh, cutting part of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh cost.

title: Utility-tunnel backside power delivery for HBM core dies
idea: Cities run utilities in tunnels under the street. Move HBM power delivery to the back of each core die with nano-TSVs and a backside power mesh, leaving every front-side TSV and bump for signals.
why: Power and ground take about half of HBM bumps and TSVs. Freeing them doubles signal density, or shrinks TSV area per bit ~30%.

title: Post-tensioned-concrete stress films enabling 15 um dies
idea: Post-tensioned concrete is pre-loaded to resist sagging. Deposit tuned compressive and tensile PECVD SiN/SiO2 films at ≤350 C on die backsides to cancel warpage, so 15 um core dies bond flat.
why: Thinner dies fit 24+ tiers within the 720 um JEDEC height and shorten TSVs, lowering capacitance and pJ/bit. That is ~1.5-2x capacity per stack.

title: Anodized-aluminum substrates with copper-filled pores replace ABF film
idea: Invert 'package dielectric must be polymer build-up film': anodize thick U.S. aluminum sheet into porous alumina whose self-ordered vertical pores are electroplated with copper to form dense vias, then pattern RDL on top.
why: Drops dependence on single-source Japanese ABF; self-forming via fields give ~1e8 vias/cm2, better thermal conduction and closer CTE match to silicon.

title: Feedback: self-tuning shared dictionaries compress traffic on both link ends
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: the memory base die and the accelerator each keep matched 256-entry value dictionaries. Repeated words (zeros, common weight and activation values) travel as 8-bit indices, and both sides update their dictionaries in lockstep each epoch using hit-rate feedback.
why: Data movement (fact 5): 1.5-3x fewer link bits per useful bit for AI tensors, cutting pJ per useful bit and bandwidth demand.

title: Lighthouse: lid-mirror free-space optical broadcast inside the package
idea: Forced link to a 'lighthouse': a VCSEL array at the center of the logic die beams upward to a curved, mirror-coated package lid, which reflects the beams down onto photodiode arrays on memory chiplets placed in a ring several cm away. No waveguides and no interposer traces are needed; each beam is a lane.
why: Escapes the shoreline/beachfront limit so 2-3x more memory chiplets fit around compute at ~1 pJ/bit over cm distances; removes large interposers.

title: Pluggable memory modules in an optical transceiver form factor
idea: MINIFY the replacement unit to a faceplate-pluggable module in an OSFP-like case holding DRAM plus a photonic link, hot-swapped like a network transceiver.
why: Memory pooled and serviceable at the rack edge; GPU packages no longer lock in memory; better utilization and repair.

title: Single optical clock broadcast removes clock-recovery from memory links
idea: Ideal: every chip already knows when each bit will arrive. Closest achievable: distribute one low-jitter mode-locked optical clock to all memory and compute chiplets through a passive splitter tree, making every link source-synchronous to a common reference with no CDR, DLL or link training.
why: Facts 5 and 7: CDR/DLL is ~20-40% of SerDes energy and area; removing it cuts link energy ~30% and lets links wake in nanoseconds instead of microseconds.

title: Ge: germanosilicate fiber delay loops hold model weights in flight
idea: Echoing mercury delay-line memory, circulate model weights as WDM light in a Ge-doped silica fiber loop (10 km ~ 50 us at 100 Tb/s ~ 600 MB in flight), re-amplified each lap and tapped at each accelerator exactly when the next layer needs those weights; the wire itself is the storage.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: weights are read cyclically every token, so sequential delay storage fits the access pattern; replaces GBs of HBM with fiber at cents per meter, energy set by amplification per lap.

title: Thread migration to the memory stack instead of data fetch
idea: Invert 'data moves to the compute': when a warp's next N accesses hit one HBM stack, the GPU ships the warp's register context (~2-8 KB) to a small SIMT island on that stack's base die and runs it there, migrating back when locality ends.
why: Moves kilobytes of state instead of megabytes of operands for pointer-chasing, graph and sparse-embedding kernels; 5-20x less off-stack traffic on those kernels, attacking the 20-25% data-movement share of accelerator power.

title: Microspring sockets for reworkable, upgradable memory dies
idea: Reverse permanent bonding: sputter stress-graded metal fingers that curl up off the interposer into 20 um-pitch microsprings, and clamp memory dies onto them, so dies can be tested, swapped or carried to the next compute generation after assembly.
why: Yield and supply: bad or worn dies are replaced instead of scrapping a whole ~$10k package, and DRAM is reused across compute generations; stressed-metal springs need only sputtering and a release etch.

title: Swappable PHY adapter chiplet keeps DRAM across generations
idea: MAGNIFY memory lifetime to three compute generations: the DRAM stack talks a fixed simple die-to-die protocol, and only a small reworkable adapter chiplet is swapped to match each new host PHY.
why: Capital and supply: memory is reused across 6-9 years instead of 3, about doubling bits served per wafer made.

title: Via-ROM weight stacks written by maskless direct-write
idea: Ideal: frozen model weights stored with zero energy and zero masks. Closest achievable: build via-programmed ROM arrays at 28 nm whose single programming via layer is written per model by multi-beam e-beam direct-write, stack 8-16 dies in an HBM footprint and hybrid-bond them to the accelerator so weights stream with no refresh and no write path.
why: Zero refresh, no capacitor (fact 1), no EUV (fact 4) and ~2-4x cheaper per bit than DRAM on depreciated 28 nm lines; frees HBM for KV cache.

title: IBM TCM revival: glass-ceramic cofired substrates replace silicon interposers
idea: Revive IBM's 1980s thermal conduction module substrate: 30-60-layer cofired glass-ceramic/copper panels, screen-printed with Cu paste and mechanically punched 50 um vias, carrying many HBM-class stacks plus logic over 100-150 mm.
why: Constraint: punching, screen printing and cofiring use no photoresist PAGs, HF or fluorinated plasma; breaks the CoWoS chokepoint on US-buildable 1980s-class tooling, with 15-20 um lines fine for wide, slower memory channels.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory packages kill refresh and wire resistance
idea: Box: 1T1C x cryo-optimized high-Vt access x SA retuned for 77 K x copper interposer at 77 K x cryostat-integrated package x standard fab. At 77 K access-transistor leakage falls by orders of magnitude so retention stretches from 64 ms to hours, and copper resistance drops ~6x so links run at lower swing.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and data movement (fact 5): near-zero refresh energy and bandwidth loss, ~3x cheaper wires; cryo-cooling overhead partly offsets.

title: Fe: magnetite-loaded underfill enables induction rework of one HBM stack
idea: Load HBM underfill and joint regions with Fe3O4 nanoparticles so a localized RF coil heats only the failing stack's joints to reflow, lifting and replacing it while the GPU and seven neighbors stay below ~100 C; package and interface are unchanged.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): rework instead of scrapping very expensive multi-stack packages; recovers the ~10-20% of packages that fail final test because of a single stack.

title: Descriptor-driven memory with no command bus
idea: MINIFY command traffic: the host writes access descriptors (stride, gather list, tile shape) once, and the base die generates every address itself, so the bus carries only data.
why: Bus efficiency and data movement: claims 20-30% effective bandwidth gain, fewer pins, and fewer row misses through on-memory scheduling.

title: Cu: hybrid-bonded 16-high DDR5 3DS stacks in standard packages
idea: Use Cu-Cu/oxide hybrid bonding (no microbumps, no underfill) to stack 16 thinned DDR5 dies within today's 3DS package height, keeping the standard DDR5 3DS ballout and RDIMM interface.
why: Density per module: 2x dies per package at the same height gives 512 GB RDIMMs from existing dies, with lower stack thermal resistance.
